snippet: On Wed, Aug 5, 2026 at 10:00 AM Nina Sokolov <nina.sokolov@habitatgoods.com> wrote: > Can make the test work. For a clean read by Oct 20 (so we have time to roll out the winner bef

On Wed, Aug 5, 2026 at 10:00 AM Nina Sokolov <nina.sokolov@habitatgoods.com> wrote:
> Can make the test work. For a clean read by Oct 20 (so we have time to roll out the winner before Nov 1) we need roughly 40K sessions per arm, which we'll clear in about 6 days at current holiday-adjacent traffic. Only catch: if the shoot direction changes because of the test, that eats into the buffer we have for finishing paid social creative. So whichever way this goes, we need final photography locked by Oct 12 at the latest.

Okay, spent yesterday building both directions properly instead of just mocking swatches, so here's a fuller writeup before we ship this to test.

Variant A (moody): pulls from the Q3 lifestyle shoot — warm, low three-quarter light, product staged in a lived-in room setting, muted sage and terracotta palette. Copy sits in a semi-transparent dark scrim so it stays legible against the darker background. This is the direction I think best represents where the brand is headed for FY27 — every competitor in the DTC home space right now is doing bright, punchy, primary-color hero banners and I think we stand out more by not doing that.

Variant B (bright): uses the Q3 PDP product photography Denise referenced — white background, high key lighting, saturated accent colors on the CTA. Copy sits on a solid color block instead of over the image, which is part of why it tests well: less visual noise competing for attention, cleaner scan path to the button.

Both variants keep the same copy hierarchy Cam wrote (headline, subhead, single CTA) so the test isolates image/palette rather than confounding it with copy changes. I also cut the confetti graphic from both per Sofia's note, and swapped 'Cozy Season Starts Here' for 'The Season, Reimagined' as the backup line since legal flagged the original — can revisit if we want something punchier once we're not worried about IP.

One more constraint worth flagging: if Variant A wins, we can ship with existing assets. If Variant B wins outright, we're mostly fine too since it's built on Q3 photography we already have licensed. Where it gets expensive is if the test comes back close and someone wants a hybrid — that would need net-new photography and we're tight on the calendar for that.

Links to both are updated in the same Figma file. Would love signoff from everyone by end of day Monday (Aug 10) so we can hand off to Nina's team with buffer before the Oct 12 photography lock she mentioned.

Rachel Lindqvist
Brand Design Lead, Habitat Goods

body_text: Jordan — running into a discrepancy building the Q3 board slide on channel performance. Finance's model, using last-touch attribution off the Shopify order data, has paid channels driving 31% of Q3 revenue. The marketing dashboard Nina's team maintains shows 48% using whatever multi-touch model is behind it. That's a big enough gap that I don't want to just pick one and hope nobody asks. subject: Re: Q3 Channel Attribution — Numbers Don't Match
snippet: On Mon, Jul 27, 2026 at 9:30 AM Wes Duffy <wes.duffy@habitatgoods.com> wrote: > Jordan — running into a discrepancy building the Q3 board slide on channel performance. Finance's mo
body_text:
On Mon, Jul 27, 2026 at 9:30 AM Wes Duffy <wes.duffy@habitatgoods.com> wrote:
> Jordan — running into a discrepancy building the Q3 board slide on channel performance. Finance's model, using last-touch attribution off the Shopify order data, has paid channels driving 31% of Q3 revenue. The marketing dashboard Nina's team maintains shows 48% using whatever multi-touch model is behind it. That's a big enough gap that I don't want to just pick one and hope nobody asks. Which number should go in the board deck, due Aug 14?

Happy to walk through why these differ, since it's a real methodology gap and not a data error on either side.

Finance's last-touch model only credits the very last click before checkout. So if a customer sees a paid social ad, doesn't click, comes back three days later through an organic search for 'Habitat Goods sectional,' and converts — that entire order gets attributed to organic search, and paid social gets zero credit, even though it's very plausibly what put the brand in front of them in the first place.

Our model is position-based: 40% credit to the first touch, 40% to the last touch, and the remaining 20% split evenly across any touches in between. Using a real example from last week — a customer's journey was: saw a Meta ad on July 19 (no click), clicked a TikTok ad on July 21, opened a retargeting email on July 23, then converted via a direct site visit on July 24 after searching the brand name. Last-touch gives 100% of that order to 'direct/organic branded search,' which tells you almost nothing useful, since the customer wouldn't have searched the brand name at all without the two paid touches earlier in the week. Our model splits that order 40% Meta, 40% TikTok, 20% email, which I'd argue is a much more honest picture of what actually drove the sale.

Neither number is 'wrong' exactly — they're answering different questions. Last-touch tells you what closed the sale. Multi-touch tells you what built the pipeline that led to the sale. The problem is using only one of them to make budget decisions, because last-touch systematically undercounts upper-funnel paid spend and multi-touch can overcount if you're not careful about the weighting.

For what it's worth, I'd push back on us reporting last-touch alone to the board — 31% badly understates what paid is actually doing for us, and if that number gets used to justify a Q4 paid budget cut, we'd be making a real strategic mistake off of an incomplete picture.

meta.action_summary: Review the multi-touch attribution methodology before it's used in the board deck.

body_text:
Heads up before this lands — a reporter at Retail Dive (Marcus Feld, no relation) is running a piece tomorrow AM on DTC packaging waste and reached out for comment on Habitat specifically. Options: (1) provide a statement, (2) decline comment, which usually reads worse in these pieces, or (3) go bigger with an interview, which I don't think we have time to prep for well given the deadline. My recommendation is a short, factual statement.

Assuming that's solid, feel free to send this over to the Fast Company reporter as our full comment, and let's explicitly decline the interview request rather than leaving it open — no upside in dragging this out with a reporter working a story that's bigger than just us anyway.
